newsitem.title: ITALY: Armed Venetian separatists say they oppose violence.
newsitem.headline: Armed Venetian separatists say they oppose violence.

text.p: The man who ordered eight armed separatists to seize the belltower in St Mark's Square in Venice last month in a bizarre independence bid told a court on Thursday the group never intended to use violence.
"We don't have a tradition of being bombers, it's not in our history or culture," said Luigi Faccia, 23, the brother of one of the eight and self-declared head of the movement.
He said the occupation had been intended as a symbolic act of liberation and the band's home-made armoured vehicle and weapons were only intended "as a deterrent".

The eight, calling themselves soldiers of the "Most Serene Republic" of Venice which was for centuries a maritime power before its fall 200 years ago, hijacked a ferry on May 9 to take them and their vehicle down the Grand Canal to St Mark's Square.
"If we had had enough money we would have also built our own ferryboat to get to St Mark's," Faccia said.
The eight had been told not to offer resistance and were ready to stay in the belltower for four days.
Instead, they were arrested within hours when police stormed the landmark and ended the siege peacefully.
They face charges including illegal arms possession, threatening public officials, kidnapping and occupying church property. They could be jailed for up to 25 years if convicted.
An element of farce entered Thursday's hearing when experts, prosecution and defence lawyers squabbled over the fire power of the armoured vehicle which the group parked in St Mark's Square.
The prosecution said a flame-thrower mounted on the vehicle was capable of firing a single blast but the defence argued that the whole armoured car would have blown up if it had been used.

Faccia, who did not take part in the operation, told the court in Mestre, just outside the famous lagoon city, that the flame-thrower was unuseable. A machinegun taken into the belltower was a World War Two relic, he added.

Defence lawyers called for the eight to be freed from jail or placed under house arrest, rather than transferred to other prisons, saying they were not dangerous and unlikely to flee. Presiding judge Graziana Campanato has yet to rule.

Outside the courtroom, police said a passer-by found a wartime hand grenade near the office of the Northern League party which wants to split the affluent north off from what it lambasts as an inefficient and corrupt Italian state.
While the party has denied involvement with the belltower stunt, its rhetoric has been blamed for inciting hot-heads.
The device was made safe but police said they did not know how it had come to light.
